extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of Reformation/early-modern European history; educated general readers interested in Erasmus and Luther
extracted.subtask_description: Close-reading and historiographical analysis of Erasmus' attitudes and actions in relation to Luther and the early Reformation (circa 1518–1521), including discussion of scholarly conduct, heresy accusations, and the boundary between reform and revolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of heresy (traditional vs contemporary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Formerly he was a heretic who differed from the Gospels or the articles of faith or from something which had an authority equal to these. Now, if anyone differ from Thomas, he is called a heretic; nay, if he differ from some new-fangled logic ... Whatever they do not like, whatever they do not understand, is heresy!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast between an older standard (deviation from Gospel or core articles of faith or equally authoritative sources) and a newer, expansive practice of branding dissent (differences from Thomas Aquinas, scholastic logic, or unfamiliar learning) as 'heresy'. Examples/anti-patterns given: condemning knowledge of Greek, speaking correctly, or unfamiliar practices as heresy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards of conduct for persons dealing with matters of faith
rubrics_metrics.description: They who deal with matters of faith ought to be far removed from every form of ambition, of money-making, of personal hatred, or of revenge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative guidance that religious actors/judges must avoid self-interested motives; invoked as a corrective to inquisitorial and factional abuses. Implies evaluation of officials by their motives as well as their doctrinal judgements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper procedure/limits for inquisitorial action
rubrics_metrics.description: If any error dangerous to Christian piety appears, it is first to be carefully worked out by the discussions of learned men and then is to be reported to the bishop. When you have done that your part as inquisitor is done. You are not called upon to stir up heaven and earth and to raise such tumults as these.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescriptive procedural standard for handling suspected doctrinal error: scholarly examination first, referral to proper ecclesiastical authorities, and avoidance of inflaming public turmoil. Cited in criticism of Hoogstraaten's handling of the Reuchlin affair as an example of improper overreach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholarly dispute etiquette (attack with superiority and modesty)
rubrics_metrics.description: We ought to fight in such fashion that we may seem to be their superiors, not only in eloquence but also in modesty and in good breeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advises critics to combine intellectual force with civility and restraint; recommends avoiding personalities and disgraceful behaviour in polemic. Example: Erasmus praising Melanchthon and urging better manners in contestation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect the value of disciplinary studies despite individual error
rubrics_metrics.description: The error of the man is to be condemned, but honour is still to be paid to his studies.... These studies do not hide the dignity of theology, but make it more plain; do not oppose it, but serve it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides theologians and ecclesiastical authorities to distinguish between condemning an individual's mistaken opinions while still recognising and honouring the intellectual discipline (languages, polite letters, music) that the individual represents. Anti-pattern: branding whole fields (e.g., languages) heretical because of individuals' errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholarly role as critic, not revolutionary leader
rubrics_metrics.description: His function was only to point out the evils and, so far as he could, to appeal to those in authority to remedy them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Norm about the proper scope of a scholar's public role: diagnose and advise rather than lead political or religious revolution. Used to explain Erasmus' cautious stance and to judge when intellectual criticism becomes political commitment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion distinguishing reformation from revolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Not merely that Luther and all who supported him refused to obey this particular decree, but that they proposed to emancipate themselves, once for all, from the control of the whole system which it represented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical test: actions amount to revolution when they reject and seek emancipation from the entire institutional/legal framework (example given: burning of papal bull and Canon Law as evidence the movement had moved from 'reformation' to 'revolution').

rubrics_metrics.name: When to resist authority vs when to endure (courage vs prudence)
rubrics_metrics.description: It isn't every one that has the strength for martyrdom...I obey the decrees of emperor and pope when they are right, because that is my duty; when they are wrong I bear it, because that is the safe plan. This I believe to be permitted even to good men if there is no hope of improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A practical ethical criterion weighing personal courage (martyrdom/resistance) against prudence and the likelihood of effective change; used to explain Erasmus' reluctance to risk his life or provoke upheaval when no plausible prospect of reform existed.
